title: Ozgur Ozel Resigns From Turkey's Main Opposition Party to Launch New Challenge Against Erdogan
excerpt: The ousted CHP leader announced his resignation in a fiery parliamentary speech, with more than 80 lawmakers expected to follow him to a new political party that polls suggest could outperform Erdogan's ruling AKP.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ozgur Ozel resigned from Turkey's CHP to form a new party challenging President Erdogan.
  • Over 80 CHP lawmakers are expected to join Ozel's new political movement.
  • A June survey shows Ozel's party could lead with 33.8% support, surpassing Erdogan's AKP at 27%.
  • The split may deepen Turkey's political crisis and affect Erdogan's potential for re-election.
  • Erdogan's AKP needs 32 more votes to call early elections amid the opposition's turmoil.

Turkey's opposition leader Ozgur Ozel announced on Tuesday that he will resign from the main opposition Republican People's Party and form a new one, marking a historic split in the century-old party founded by modern Turkey's founder Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. The move comes amid a nearly two-year legal crackdown on President Tayyip Erdogan's political opponents that has rattled financial markets and drawn criticism from the European Union.

"Today, we are on the brink of a sad farewell that has become inevitable and whose time has come. However, we would like to share with the people that we carry the hope of a new beginning."

— Ozgur Ozel, Ousted CHP Chairman

A Forced Exit From Ataturk's Party

In a fiery speech before more than 80 CHP lawmakers in parliament, Ozel said the resignation did not mean they were succumbing to political pressure, but rather embarking on a new kind of opposition to Erdogan, who has run Turkey for more than two decades, according to Reuters.

The move was precipitated by a May court decision that annulled the CHP's 2023 congress, citing irregularities, and reinstated former leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu as chairman. Kilicdaroglu lost to Erdogan in the 2023 presidential election. Ozel and critics called the ruling a politically motivated "coup" that was part of a broader legal crackdown on the opposition.

Most CHP voters and parliamentarians are expected to follow Ozel to the new, as-yet unnamed party. Turkish media have reported that as many as 73 CHP lawmakers could resign to join an Ozel-led movement, according to Turkish Minute. At least 90 of the CHP's 135 lawmakers are believed to back Ozel.

> **"Turkish media have reported that as many as 73 CHP lawmakers could resign to join an Ozel-led movement, according to Turkish Minute."** ![President Erdogan. Key Takeaways Ozgur Ozel resigned from Turkey's CHP to form a new party challenging President Erdogan.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/ba/Turkish_President_Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan_in_January_2024_%28cropped%29.jpg)

Poll Numbers Favor Ozel

A MetroPOLL survey conducted in June found that an Ozel-led party would rank first in a hypothetical parliamentary election with 33.8 percent of the vote, ahead of Erdogan's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) at 27 percent, according to Turkish Minute. The CHP under Kilicdaroglu measured at just 5 percent — below the 7 percent threshold required to enter parliament.

The numbers underscore the scale of the realignment underway. Without the hypothetical split scenario, the AKP stood at 31.1 percent and the CHP at 27.5 percent in the same survey measuring current party preferences.

![Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/Ataturk1930s.jpg)

Two Years of Crackdown

The opposition's crisis is rooted in a sustained legal offensive that began in October 2024, when the CHP mayor of Istanbul's Esenyurt district was jailed over alleged links to the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). Since then, hundreds of CHP members and officials have been detained or investigated on corruption and other charges that the party denies.

The crisis escalated sharply in March 2025 with the jailing of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, Erdogan's main political rival, triggering Turkey's largest protests in a decade and a sharp market selloff, Reuters reported. Imamoglu faces charges ranging from graft to espionage and terrorism, which he denies. His university diploma was also annulled, rendering him ineligible to run for the presidency.

More than 30 CHP mayors have been arrested, removed from office, or replaced by government-appointed trustees since the March 2024 local elections, according to BBC Turkish. The government denies targeting the opposition and maintains that the judiciary acts independently.

What It Means for Erdogan and Turkey's Elections

The opposition's splintering could boost Erdogan's prospects of extending his rule. Under Turkey's constitution, Erdogan has reached his two-term presidential limit but can run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term. A three-fifths majority of 360 of 600 lawmakers is required to call an early vote.

Erdogan's AKP and its allies currently hold 328 seats, needing 32 more votes. Some analysts say the ruling alliance might seek support from the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, which has 63 seats and has since late 2024 helped facilitate steps toward peace between the Turkish state and the PKK, according to Reuters.

The next elections are scheduled for May 14, 2028, but analysts say they could come earlier if the government seeks to capitalize on the CHP's internal crisis.

Political Landscape Shift
›More than 80 lawmakers expected to join Ozel.
›CHP's internal crisis could benefit Erdogan's re-election chances.
›Erdogan's AKP currently holds 328 seats in parliament.
›Early elections could be called if Erdogan gains support.

What to Watch

The key questions now are how quickly Ozel can formally register his new party, how many CHP lawmakers and voters follow him, and whether the split weakens or ultimately strengthens the opposition's challenge to Erdogan. The EU and international markets will be watching closely for signals on Turkey's democratic trajectory. Erdogan's allies have floated a constitutional amendment as another path to extending his rule, but polls suggest the public is divided on the issue.
